                                        PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE               §           PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS              §
 UNDER PURA 37.0561                          §                      OF TEXAS


               COMMENTS OF CENTERPOINT ENERGY HOUSTON ELECTRIC, LLC

       CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (“CenterPoint Energy” or the “Company”) is a

transmission and distribution utility (“TDU”) that interconnects large load (“LL”) customers and

submits these comments on the Proposal for Publication filed on March 12, 2026. The Proposal

for Publication seeks to adopt a new rule governing the LL customer interconnection process to

be codified at 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.194 and is intended to establish the interconnection

standards mandated in PURA § 37.0561 as enacted by SB 6 during the 2025 regular legislative

session. PURA § 37.0561 requires the Commission to establish standards for interconnecting LL

customers in the ERCOT power region. The Commission has requested comments from interested

persons on its proposal by April 17, 2026. Below are CenterPoint Energy’s general and subsection

specific comments.

                                   I.      General Comments

       The most significant concerns that CenterPoint Energy has with the proposed rule are

highlighted in this section. Those concerns are:

A. The payment of the interconnection fee and CIAC and the provision of financial securities
   should be due 30 days after, rather than on, the agreement’s execution date, and parties
   should have up to 60 days after the study’s completion to execute an interconnection
   agreement.
B. The dollar per MW interconnection fee should not discourage businesses wanting to come to
   or expand in Texas, be set based on the size of the customer’s load, and returned to the LL
   customer as it achieves certain commercial development milestones.
C. The ambiguity of whether LL customer interconnections directly to a TDU distribution system
   are outside the scope of PURA § 37.0561 and the proposed rule should be clarified.



                                                                                                1
 D. A stand-alone financial security for procurement of significant equipment and services should
   not be required under an interconnection agreement, since all procurement costs will be
   covered by the CAIC and the system upgrade financial security.
E. The broad definition for direct interconnection costs and lack of definition for system upgrade
   costs makes it difficult for TDUs to properly categorize its incurred interconnection costs.
F. The interconnection fee and financial security should not be used to reduce the amount of a
   TDU’s invested capital included rate base and instead should be returned to the LL customer.
G. The interconnection fee and CIAC must be grossed up for taxes to the extent that they
   constitute taxable income, to cover the TDU’s tax liability resulting from the receipt of those
   funds.
H. The term “site” used in the large load customer definition should itself be defined as having
   the same meaning as “premises” in the pro forma tariff of all TDUs.
I. The Commission should approve a standard form of the required intermediate agreement and
   a standard form of the required interconnection agreement.

A.     The payment of the interconnection fee and CIAC and the provision of financial
       securities should be due up to 30 days after, rather than on, the agreement’s execution
       date, and parties should have up to 60 days after the study’s completion to execute an
       interconnection agreement.

       As the TDU serving the Greater Houston area containing a number of traditional energy

and manufacturing businesses, in addition to the data centers that are driving the large load

conversations across the state, CenterPoint Energy is concerned that the timelines being

proposed for large load interconnections will be challenging for many of the Company’s

traditional large load customers who are seeking to expand or build new load facilities. Based on

the Company’s experience, requiring large load customers to pay the interconnection fee and

contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) and furnish the required financial securities on or

before the date that the interconnection agreement is executed may not be feasible. A large load

customer may need and should have up to 30 days after the interconnection agreement is

executed to provide the required interconnection fee, CIAC, and financial securities. Also, the

parties should have up to 60 days after completion of the interconnection study (rather than 30

days) to execute an interconnection agreement to give them sufficient time to review the study


                                                2

                                                                                                2
 results and negotiate the terms of the interconnection agreement, especially in the absence of a

Commission-approved, standard form interconnection agreement.

B.       The dollar per MW interconnection fee, if retained, should be restructured based on the
         customers load and allowed to be returned to the LL customer upon achievement of
         certain commercial development milestones.

         To support business development and be consistent with PURA § 37.0561, the Company

believes that the dollar per MW amount for the interconnection fee should be refundable, and

the amount of the fee should be based on the demand level of the interconnecting customer’s

load. The Company proposes the following tiered structure for the interconnection fee:

     •   $10,000 per MW for 75-250 MW loads
     •   $20,000 per MW for 251-1,000 MW loads
     •   $30,000 per MW for greater than 1,000 MW loads and capped at $50 million

         Importantly, the interconnection fee (at least to the extent not needed to cover any

outstanding interconnection costs owed by the LL customer) should be returned to the LL

customer as it achieves certain commercial development milestones. Those milestones should

be designed to incentivize LL customers to see their projects through to completion and reach

their full contracted peak demand. In this regard, CenterPoint Energy proposes the following

milestones as triggers for a graduated refund of the interconnection fee:

     •   Upon initial energization of the project, 50% of the total interconnection fee paid should
         be refunded by the TDU to the LL customer.
     •   Upon achievement of half of the LL customer’s contracted peak demand, 25% of the total
         interconnection fee paid should be refunded by the TDU to the LL customer.
     •   Upon achievement of the other half of the LL customer’s contracted peak demand, the
         remaining 25% of the total interconnection fee paid should be refunded by the TDU to the
         LL customer.

         If a customer does not achieve a milestone, the amount that would have been refunded

had the milestone been reached should be applied by the TDU to cover any outstanding amounts


                                                 3

                                                                                                 3
 owed for system upgrade costs (and thereby reduce the amount of such costs that would have

otherwise been rate base eligible).

C.       The ambiguity of whether LL customer interconnections directly to a TDU distribution
         system are outside the scope of PURA § 37.0561 and the proposed rule should be
         clarified.

         PURA § 37.0561 appears to be intended to only address LL customer interconnections to

the ERCOT transmission system. This intention is based on the fact that many of the “standards

for interconnecting large load customers” that the legislature directed the Commission to

establish can be applied only to LL customer interconnections to the ERCOT transmission system

and would not be applicable to LL customer interconnections directly to distribution systems

within ERCOT. Like the statute, the proposed rule also appears intended to cover only LL customer

interconnections to the ERCOT transmission system.             CenterPoint Energy requests the

Commission to confirm that the scope of the rule is limited to only LL customer interconnections

to the ERCOT transmission system and is not intended to cover LL customer interconnections

directly to distribution systems in the ERCOT power region.

D.       A stand-alone financial security for procurement of significant equipment and services
         should not be required under an interconnection agreement, since all procurement
         costs will be covered by the CAIC and the system upgrade financial security.

         Subsection (f)(8) of the proposed rule requires a LL customer to post a “financial security

for significant equipment or services” upon its execution of an interconnection agreement.

However, all interconnection costs, including procurement costs, fall into one of only two

categories:

     •   Customer Costs. Costs for the engineering, procurement, and construction of facilities

         needed to interconnect and provide delivery service to a customer, which should be


                                                  4

                                                                                                  4
          recovered from the customer as a CIAC if these facilities provide no transmission system

         benefits to anyone other than the interconnected customer, and

     •   Rate Base Costs. Costs for the engineering, procurement, and construction of facilities

         needed to interconnect and provide delivery service to a customer, which should be

         recovered through the TDU’s delivery service rates if these facilities are used and useful

         to increase the availability, capacity, or reliability of utility service on the existing

         transmission system.

A stand-alone financial security for equipment procurement costs has no purpose in

interconnection agreements, because all equipment procurement costs are either included in the

CIAC or covered by the system upgrade security.

E.       The broad definition for direct interconnection costs and lack of definition for system
         upgrade costs could make it difficult for a TDU to properly categorize its incurred
         interconnection costs.

         The proposed rule requires a LL customer to pay a CIAC for all direct interconnection costs,

defined as “all costs associated with facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the

existing ERCOT system, including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect

the new large load customer.” Under this definition, the CIAC seems to encompass the costs that

a TDU would incur to engineer, procure, and construct all interconnection facilities. It is not clear

what other interconnection facilities are intended to be covered by the financial security for

significant equipment and the financial security for system upgrades, especially since system

upgrades is not defined. Direct interconnection costs should be defined as the engineering,

procurement, and construction (“EPC”) cost of facilities needed to interconnect the customer that

are beneficial and used and useful only for that customer. System upgrade costs, on the other


                                                  5

                                                                                                   5
 hand, should be defined as the EPC cost of facilities needed to interconnect the customer that

are also beneficial and used and useful to the transmission system, or for the reliability or

availability of transmission service, generally.

       Direct interconnection costs should be paid by the LL customer requesting

interconnection via the CIAC. System upgrade costs should be eligible for inclusion in the

interconnecting TDU’s transmission rate base and recovered through its rates for transmission

service and should not constitute interconnection costs owed by the LL customer who

successfully energizes and uses the transmission capacity constructed for the interconnection.

F.     The interconnection fee and financial security should not be used to reduce the amount
       of a TDU’s invested capital included rate base and instead should be returned to the LL
       customer.

       Subsection (f)(7) of the proposed rule requires a TDU to apply the interconnection fee as

an offset to its transmission rate base. Subsections (g) and (h) of the proposed rule likewise

require a TDU to apply the financial securities received under an interconnection agreement as

an offset to its transmission rate base if the LL customer withdraws its contracted peak demand

before the interconnection is energized or if the LL customer fails to satisfy a phased energization

milestone after the interconnection is energized, respectively.

       Any funds received by a TDU under an interconnection agreement with a LL customer

should be used only to cover the cost of the interconnection. Any remaining balances should be

returned to the LL customer. There is no authority in PURA § 37.0561 for the Commission to

direct TDUs to use those funds to subsidize the transmission cost of service for all.

G.     The interconnection fee and CIAC must be grossed up for taxes to the extent that they
       constitute taxable income, to cover the TDU’s tax liability resulting from the receipt of
       those funds.


                                                   6

                                                                                                  6
         Both the subsections (f)(7) non-refundable interconnection fee and (f)(9) CIAC that a LL

customer must pay to the interconnecting TDU under an interconnection agreement may

represent taxable income of the TDU and, therefore, create a tax liability for the TDU. To cover

this liability, the amounts required from the LL customer to satisfy these financial requirements

must be grossed up by the TDU. The interconnection rule adopted by the Commission should

explicitly allow the interconnecting TDUs to gross up the interconnection fee and CIAC amounts

to cover this tax liability.

H.      The term “site” used in the large load customer definition should itself be defined as
        having the same meaning as “premises” in the pro forma tariff of all TDUs.

        In the Commission’s pro forma tariff for retail delivery service adopted in 16 TAC § 25.214,

which is used by all TDUs in the ERCOT region, the term “premises” is defined as “A tract of land

or real estate or related commonly used tracts, including buildings and other appurtenances

thereon.” Subsection (c) of the proposed rule defines a LL customer as “An entity requesting a

new or expanded interconnection where the customer’s total expected non-coincident peak

demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 MW” (emphasis added). The Company believes

that the word “site” in the rule and the word “premises” in the pro forma tariff for retail delivery

services should have the same meanings. Additionally, a single premises may have more than

one service delivery points1 that are nevertheless served by a shared or common transmission

circuit, in which case all service delivery points on the premises that are served by a common

transmission circuit under a single ESI ID should be counted as a single large load customer for




1
  “Service delivery point” is the ERCOT term for describing where electricity “flows from the [TDU] to a load
customer.” The Commission uses the term “point of delivery” to describe where electricity “leaves the delivery
system.”

                                                      7

                                                                                                            7
 study purposes. This may help to reduce the potential for uncertainty and ambiguity in

determining if different loads should be counted as a single load for purposes of making a “large

load customer” designation.

I.     The Commission should approve a standard form of the required intermediate
       agreement and a standard form of the required interconnection agreement.

       The proposed rule mandates that both the subsection (d) intermediate agreement and

the subsection (f) interconnection agreement must “meet the requirements” of those respective

subsections. To prevent challenges to these agreements based on whether they satisfy these

requirements, and to promote uniformity across ERCOT, the Commission should approve the

standard form of these agreements that must be used for LL interconnections throughout ERCOT.

The requirements listed in subsections (d) and (f) that must be satisfied do not easily translate

into contract provisions that can be drafted and inserted into these agreements, creating

unnecessary regulatory risk to TDUs and their LL customers that their agreements might be found

to have failed to satisfy those requirements.

                           II.    SUBSECTION SPECIFIC COMMENTS

       The Company’s observations concerning specific subsections in the proposed rule are

discussed below.

       A.      Subsection (a) Purpose and Scope.

       As discussed above, the purpose and scope of this rule seems to be limited to large load

customer interconnections to the ERCOT transmission system.            The Company requests

Commission confirmation that it does not intend for this rule to apply to large load customer

interconnections directly to distribution systems within the ERCOT power region. If it is the



                                                8

                                                                                               8
 Commission’s intent that this should apply to distribution system interconnections, the Company

believes that the rule will require substantial modifications to accomplish such an intent.

       The scope of both PURA § 37.0561 and the proposed rule seems to exclude LL customer

interconnections (75 MW or larger) directly to distribution systems within the ERCOT power

region. Both the statute and the proposed rule assume that all LL customer interconnections will

be to the ERCOT transmission system. Nevertheless, CenterPoint Energy has received multiple

customer interconnection requests of 75 MW or larger that seek interconnection directly to the

Company’s distribution system.

       PURA § 37.0561 appears to be intended to only address LL customer interconnections to

the ERCOT transmission system. This intention is based on the fact that many of the “standards

for interconnecting large load customers” that the legislature directed the Commission to

establish can be applied only to LL customer interconnections to the ERCOT transmission system

and would not be applicable to LL customer interconnections directly to distribution systems

within ERCOT. For example, the financial commitment standard that the legislature directed the

Commission to establish under PURA § 37.0561(h) is expressly limited to financial commitments

“for the development of transmission infrastructure needed to serve a large load customer”

(emphasis added). The statute is silent about financial commitments for the development of

distribution infrastructure needed to serve large load customers. The direct interconnection

costs for a distribution system interconnection request, however, would consist predominantly, if

not entirely, of distribution infrastructure costs.

       Moreover, the statute’s interconnection standard for on-site backup generation that the

legislature directed the Commission to establish under PURA § 37.0561(e) is also limited to LL


                                                      9

                                                                                               9
 customer interconnections with the ERCOT transmission system. As part of this standard, the

legislature directed ERCOT to “establish a threshold before or during an energy emergency alert

at which [it] may issue reasonable notice” requiring a LL customer with on-site backup generating

facilities “to either deploy the customer’s on-site backup generating facilities or curtail load.”

ERCOT, however, does not have the authority or the capability to require distribution system load

customers with on-site backup generation to either deploy their backup generation or curtail their

load before or during an energy emergency alert. This requirement, therefore, must necessarily

be limited to the interconnection of transmission system load customers with on-site backup

generation and must necessarily exclude the interconnection of distribution system load

customer with on-site backup generation.

       Like the statute, the proposed rule is completely silent about distribution infrastructure

cost responsibility, indicating that the Commission’s intention is for the rule to cover only LL

customer interconnections to the ERCOT transmission system. For example, subsection (a) of the

proposed rule expressly limits the rule’s purpose and scope to LL customer interconnections only

“to the ERCOT system,” which would make LL customer interconnections directly to a TDU’s

distribution systems seemingly fall outside of the rule’s purpose and scope. In addition,

subsections (f)(7), (g), and (h) of the proposed rule all state that any balances remaining under,

respectively, the interconnection fee and financial securities required for an interconnection

agreement must be applied “as an offset” to the TDU’s transmission rate base, implicitly

assuming that all LL customer interconnections are to the transmission system (with no offset to

be applied to the TDU’s distribution rate base, which should be the case for LL customer

interconnections to a TDU’s distribution system). Finally, the definitions in proposed subsection


                                               10

                                                                                               10
 (c) for the terms “interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP)”2 and “interconnecting

distribution service provider (DSP)”3 show a clear determination that the rule considers only the

interconnecting TSP, not the interconnecting DSP, to be the entity that “owns and operates the

facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.”4

         In light of these factors, CenterPoint Energy requests the Commission to confirm that the

purpose and scope of the rule is limited exclusively to LL customer interconnections to the ERCOT

transmission system and is not intended to cover LL customer interconnections directly to

individual DSP distribution systems in the ERCOT power region. If the Commission believes that

the rule is intended to also cover LL customer interconnections to individual DSP distribution

systems in the ERCOT power region, then the Company requests that the Commission clarify that

the rules to unambiguously cover such interconnections. Further, the Company requests that the

Commission also direct ERCOT to determine if and under what conditions these types of

interconnections need to be included in ERCOT’s LLIS process or whether a separate process

should be used or developed to analyze their potential transmission system impacts.

         B.       Subsection (b) Applicability.

         CenterPoint Energy recommends the following changes to subsection (b) to clarify the

applicability of the rule:

         This section applies to a retail customer or developer that seeks:

3

and operator of the facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the distribution system (which

                 (1) a new interconnection of a retail customer load that is equal to or
                exceeds 75 megawatts (MW) at a single site;
                (2) any retail customer load increase at an existing non-large load customer
                an expanded interconnection site that causes the cumulative load at the
                site to equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and
                (3) any retail customer load increase at an existing large load customer an
                expanded interconnection site of that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.

        C.      Subsection (c) Definitions.

                1.      Backup generating facilities.     The definition of “backup generating

facilities” omits the requirement in PURA § 37.0561(e) that defines such facilities as being able to

“serve at least 50 percent of on-site demand.”

                2.      Competitively sensitive information. The definition of “competitively

sensitive information” includes “compute-deployment strategies.” The Company requests that

the Commission clarify what this means.

        Competitively sensitive information would also include “commercial terms.”              The

Company believes that every term in an intermediate agreement and interconnection agreement

may be a commercial term, including terms covering financial securities and CIAC. On the other

hand, the definition of competitively sensitive information would exclude “the identity of a large

load customer; general site location, . . . requested or contracted peak demand; timing of

energization; or whether an interconnection request is associated with the same applicant or

affiliated entities.”   Excluding those terms from the definition of “competitively sensitive

information,” however, does not exclude those terms from the definition of “proprietary

customer information” under 16 TAC § 25.272(c)(5), which includes, among other things, a

customer’s “expected patterns of use,” “individual contract terms and conditions,” and “any other

information that the customer expressly requested not be disclosed.” (Emphasis added). The

                                                 12

                                                                                                 12
 existing definition for “proprietary customer information” is therefore much broader than the

proposed definition for “competitively sensitive information” and includes the information that

would be excluded from the latter’s definition. Lastly, the Company notes a possible conflict

between subsection (d)(2)(D) of the proposed rule, which requires ERCOT to “treat disclosed

competitively sensitive information as Protected Information under ERCOT protocols,” and 16 TAC

§ 25.272(g)(1) of the Commission’s existing rules, which requires ERCOT to treat disclosed

proprietary customer information in accordance with “the rules in this subsection with respect to

releasing the information to other persons.”

                  3.       Large load customer. Finally, as discussed in the above summary, the word

“site” that is used in the definition of “large load customer” should be defined as having the same

meaning as the word “premises” that is used in the Commission’s pro forma tariff for retail

delivery service adopted in 16 TAC § 25.214, which is used by all TDUs in the ERCOT region.

“Premises” is defined in the pro forma tariff as “a tract of land or real estate or related commonly

used tracts, including buildings and other appurtenances thereon.” The proposed rule defines a

LL customer as “an entity5 requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the customer’s

total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 MW”

(emphasis added). The Company believes that the word “site” in the rule and the word

“premises” in the pro forma tariff for retail delivery services should have the same meanings.




5
  Instead of “entity,” the definition of LL customer should use the term “retail customer” as defined in the pro forma
tariff adopted by the Commission in § 25.214 of its rules. In the pro forma tariff, the definition of “retail customer”
includes not only the “end-use customer who purchases [electricity] and ultimately consumes it,” but also includes
(“in the context of Construction Services,” which is exactly the context of the proposed new rule) “property owners,
builders, developers, [and] contractors.” A large load customer, whether an end-user or a developer, is a retail
customer as defined in the pro forma tariff.

                                                                                                                    13
 Additionally, a single premises may have more than one service delivery points 6 that are

nevertheless served by a shared or common transmission circuit, in which case all service delivery

points on the premises that are served by a common transmission circuit under a single ESI ID

should be counted as a single large load customer for study purposes. This may help to reduce

the potential for uncertainty and ambiguity in determining if different loads should be counted

as a single load for purposes of making a “large load customer” designation.

        D.       Subsection (d) Intermediate Agreement.

                 1.       Standard form of agreement.                  Subsection (d) requires that each

intermediate agreement “must meet the requirements of this subsection.” This mandate is vague

and ambiguous to the Company. There is significant uncertainty in drafting contract provisions

designed to meet those requirements. For example, the requirements listed in the rule that an

intermediate agreement must meet include the requirement that the customer “must

demonstrate site control [via] a signed and executed lease agreement . . . a deed . . . or a signed

and executed agreement with an option to purchase or lease. . . .” To satisfy this requirement,

the parties to an intermediate agreement must negotiate, draft, and insert a demonstration-of-

site-control provision into their agreement. The Company is not sure how to convert this

demonstration-of-site-control requirement into contract language, or if the deed or other

evidence of site control must itself be attached to and made a part of the intermediate

agreement.




6
  “Service delivery point” is the ERCOT term for describing where electricity “flows from the [TDU delivery system]
to a load customer.” The Commission’s rules use the term “point of delivery” for describing where electricity “leaves
the [TDU] delivery system” and flows to a retail customer.

                                                         14

                                                                                                                  14
          The same problem is presented with trying to draft contract language that satisfies the

other intermediate agreement requirements, including contract language that satisfies the

requirement that the customer disclose (1) if it is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection

request and, if so, all the additional information required associated with the substantially similar

interconnection request; (2) its plans and progress for obtaining site-related studies and

engineering services, plus a separate attestation concerning such plans and progress; (3) its plans

and progress for obtaining “non-ministerial discretionary approvals . . . required . . . before

energization,”7 plus a separate attestation concerning such plans and progress;8 (4) how it plans

to procure power and whether it has on-site generation; and (5) whether it can be modeled as a

controllable load resource. In the Company’s opinion, these disclosures should be made in an

affidavit that the customer should have to submit to the interconnecting TDU as part of the

customer’s application for interconnection. In any event, to promote uniformity across ERCOT

and reduce the significant regulatory risk and uncertainty of having an intermediate agreement

challenged for failing to meet the subsection (d) requirements, the Company believes that the

rule adopted in this rulemaking project should include the standard form of the intermediate

agreement that parties in ERCOT must use for large load customer interconnections.

                  2.       Study fee. Subsection (d) also requires the intermediate agreement to

cover the study fee. The study fee for customers seeking transmission system interconnection

has always been and continues to be covered by a separate study fee agreement. There is no

 reason to discontinue that practice. The real purpose of an intermediate agreement should

limited to addressing the customer’s provision of the dollar per MW financial security and, if

applicable, a financial security for the procurement of significant equipment.

       E.      Subsection (e) Interconnection Study.

       Subsection (e)(4) of the proposed rule effectively terminates a large load customer’s

interconnection request if, after initiation of the interconnection study, the customer requests

any amount of additional capacity for the interconnection. There should be a de minimis

exception for a requested capacity increase that would not trigger termination of the original

request. Moreover, while subsection (e)(4) currently would apply only to requested increases to

the amount of interconnection capacity originally requested, it should equally apply to requested

decreases to the amount of the capacity originally requested.

       F.      Subsection (f) Interconnection Agreement.

               1.     Standard form of agreement. Similar to subsection (d)’s mandate that

each intermediate agreement “must meet the requirements” of that subsection, Subsection (f)

also mandates that each interconnection agreement “must meet the requirements of this

subsection.” For the reasons discussed above concerning the intermediate agreement, the

Company believes that the rule adopted in this rulemaking project should include the standard

form of the interconnection agreement that parties in ERCOT must use for large load customer

interconnections.

               2.     Interconnection agreement due dates. Subsections (f)(7) and (f)(9) of the

proposed rule require an LL customer to pay the interconnection fee and CIAC, respectively, “not




                                               16

                                                                                              16
 later than the date that the interconnection agreement is executed.” 9 Likewise, subsections (f)(8)

and (f)(10) of the proposed rule require a LL customer to provide a financial security for significant

equipment or services and a financial security for system upgrades, respectively, “not later than

the date that the interconnection agreement is executed.”10

        The Company understands the concerns the Commission is attempting to address with

the payment-due-upon-execution deadline, but if the Commission requires such payments and

securities to be paid by the LL customer on or prior to the agreement’s execution, it could have

the unintended consequences of making Texas less competitive. The Company agrees that the

funding for the interconnection must be provided prior to a TDU’s commencement of EPC work

on the LL customer interconnection but not necessarily on the execution date of the

interconnection agreement.           The interconnection project becomes a “go” project for the

interconnecting TDU (meaning, the TDU will commence incurring EPC costs on the project) only

after the financial commitments made by the customer in the interconnection agreement have

been delivered to the TDU. Further, it has been the Company’s experience in its interactions with

both prospective customers who are seeking to build new load facilities in the Company’s service

area and for existing customers who may seek to expand their business in our service area, that

due to a variety of customer specific facts and/or financial circumstances, that some customers

may need time after contract execution to finalize the necessary financial arrangements with their

delivered at the same time as the CIAC.

 financial institutions. While some customers may be able to deliver payments on the day the

agreement is executed, it has been the company’s experience that even large national or global

companies may not be able to physically deliver these financial commitments on the same day

that they execute the agreement.      The Commission should therefore allow a LL customer a

reasonable amount of time, up to at least 30 days after the execution of the agreement, to deliver

these financial commitments.

       Subsection (f) also requires an interconnection agreement’s execution to occur “not later

than 30 days after completion of the interconnection study.” The Company believes the execution
